title: EAQGA: A Quantum-Enhanced Genetic Algorithm with Novel Entanglement-Aware Crossovers
abstract_summary: The paper proposes EAQGA, a quantum-enhanced genetic algorithm that introduces an entanglement-aware crossover to encode correlated bit pairs from elite solutions into shallow quantum circuits, using a limited number of entanglements to remain NISQ-friendly. The method is applied to portfolio optimization and evaluated on simulators and IBM's 127-qubit ibm_quebec device, reporting substantially improved fitness (≈33–37% better) over classical GA and a quantum-inspired GA under the same iteration and population settings.
methodology_description: The authors propose an entanglement-aware quantum-enhanced genetic algorithm (EAQGA) for binary combinatorial optimization (QUBO) problems and evaluate it on portfolio optimization. Solutions are encoded as measured bitstrings of quantum circuits whose qubits correspond to decision variables (one qubit per asset). Each generation: (1) N circuits are prepared from an initial |+> superposition (Hadamards) and measured to obtain an initial population; (2) an elitism pool of the top two solutions is maintained; (3) new circuits for the next generation are produced by a crossover that (a) detects correlated bit-pairs between the two elite parents (positive or negative correlations approximating Bell-state patterns), (b) probabilistically selects pairs for entanglement using a selection probability ps modulated by the normalized covariance entries and a time-dependent decay factor df(t), (c) builds short entanglement chains and encodes selected correlations into circuits using RY rotations on control qubits and CNOTs (or RY+X+CNOT for negative correlations), and (d) biases non-entangled qubits toward elite-bit values by single-qubit RY rotations with probability parameter pa; (4) each generated circuit is measured once in the computational basis, solutions evaluated by the Min-Var (mean-variance) QUBO objective µ^T x - q x^T Σ x (q=0.5), and the elitism pool updated. The algorithm is run for a fixed number of iterations with fixed population sizes. Comparative baselines include a classical GA and an adaptive quantum-inspired GA (AQGA). Experiments use Qiskit tooling, a Matrix Product State (MPS) simulator for circuits with limited entanglement, and experiments on real hardware (IBM ibm_quebec). Performance is reported as average and standard deviation of fitness values over repeated runs and compared to baselines and brute-force optimum (where tractable).
frameworks: Qiskit (Qiskit Sampler, Qiskit Finance DataProvider, Qiskit Aer MPS)
experimental_setup: Simulations used the Qiskit Matrix Product State (MPS) simulator (Qiskit Aer). Real-device experiments used IBM Quantum’s 127-qubit processor ibm_quebec (access via PINQ2). Problem sizes: subsets of 30 and 40 assets on simulator (10 different subsets each), and a 100-asset subset on the real device. Population sizes: 10 and 20 (simulator), 10 (hardware). Iterations: 20. Each circuit was measured once (shots=1).
dataset_used: Historical daily price data for S&P 500 constituent stocks obtained via Qiskit Finance (YahooDataProvider). Time range: 2023-10-01 to 2024-09-30. Returns computed as Pit/Pit-1 - 1; per-asset mean µ and covariance Σ computed from these returns. The portfolio objective used a binary Mean-Variance QUBO with risk-aversion q = 0.5. Random non-overlapping subsets of 30 and 40 assets were used for simulator runs; one random subset of 100 assets used on hardware.

experiment_input.preprocessing: Compute daily returns Rit = Pit/Pit-1 - 1; µ_i = mean(Rit); Σ_{i,j} = sample covariance using T-1 denominator
experiment_input.problem_encoding: Binary QUBO objective: maximize µ^T x - q x^T Σ x with q=0.5; one qubit per asset

experiment_process.initialization: Prepare circuits in |0>^n, apply Hadamard to each qubit to create |+>^n; measure to generate initial population (N circuits).
experiment_process.elitism: Maintain top two solutions (elitism pool) per iteration to guide crossover.
experiment_process.crossover_generation: For each new circuit: detect correlated index pairs between the two elite parents (positive/negative correlations). Compute selection probability p_s = ps * (possibly df(t)) * |Σ_n(i,j)| with decay factor df(t) = 0.5 + t/(2*Tmax). Probabilistically select pairs, form entanglement chains, choose one qubit as control and others targets, encode pairwise/chain correlations using RY rotations on control(s), CNOT(s), and X for negative-type correlations. For non-entangled qubits, apply single-qubit RY to bias measurement toward elite-bit with amplitude pa.
experiment_process.measurement: Measure each circuit once in the computational basis (shots=1) to obtain a candidate bitstring.
experiment_process.evaluation: Compute fitness using QUBO objective µ^T x - q x^T Σ x; update elitism pool and repeat for Tmax iterations.
experiment_process.baselines_and_comparisons: Classical GA (roulette selection, single-point crossover p=0.85, mutation rate=0.03), AQGA (adaptive rotation scheme with θmax=0.25, θmin=0.15, mutation ratio=0.05, disaster operation reinitializing worst 20% after 6 stagnant iterations).
experiment_process.runs_and_repetition: Simulator: each algorithm run 100 times per subset to compute mean and std. Hardware: experiments repeated 10 times for the 100-asset subset.

experiment_output.metric: Fitness value defined by the QUBO objective (Mean-Variance: µ^T x - q x^T Σ x). Tables present values multiplied by 100 for readability.
experiment_output.statistics_reported: Average and standard deviation of fitness across repeated runs; improvement percentages versus baselines reported (e.g., EAQGA 33.6% better than GA and 37.2% better than AQGA on the 100-asset hardware experiment).
baselines: Brute-force optimum (reported where tractable for small subsets)
experiment_output.output_format: Per-iteration average fitness curves and final average/std fitness tables across subsets and population sizes

No public code repository or notebook link is provided in the manuscript. Data are publicly accessible via Yahoo Finance through Qiskit Finance. Reproduction of hardware experiments requires access to IBM Quantum backends (ibm_quebec) and the same Qiskit primitives; exact circuit-generation seeds and implementation code are not provided, which may hinder exact replication.
key_findings: [supported] The proposed Entanglement-Aware Quantum-Enhanced Genetic Algorithm (EAQGA) outperforms a classical Genetic Algorithm (GA) and an Adaptive Quantum-Inspired Genetic Algorithm (AQGA) on the tested portfolio-optimization instances (simulator experiments, sizes 30 and 40, populations 10 and 20).

[supported] On real quantum hardware (IBM ibm_quebec, using 100 qubits / a 100-asset subset) EAQGA produced average fitness values 33.6% better than GA and 37.2% better than AQGA under the reported experimental conditions (20 iterations, population size 10).
[supported] EAQGA yielded lower standard deviations (i.e., higher empirical stability) across repeated runs than GA and AQGA in the reported experiments.

[supported] The new crossover encodes observed bit-pair correlations from elite solutions into shallow quantum circuits via a heuristic that maps positive/negative correlations to small entangled subcircuits (CNOT + RY pattern) and biases single qubits with RY rotations.

[speculative] Limiting the number of entangled pairs and keeping circuit depth shallow makes the method especially suitable for NISQ devices and reduces noise-related degradation in practice (asserted but not proven as a general rule across hardware/noise models).
[supported] The authors explicitly state they do not claim a formal quantum advantage; because the algorithm uses limited entanglement, it remains classically simulable in many cases.

[speculative] Encoding entanglement patterns (|ψp⟩ and |ψn⟩ style correlations) is argued to capture economically meaningful joint behaviors (e.g., mutually exclusive or jointly-selected asset pairs) and thereby aid portfolio optimization; this mapping is plausible but presented as an algorithmic/interpretive claim rather than a proven theorem.
[supported] EAQGA performs comparatively well even with small population sizes (e.g., population = 10), outperforming GA and AQGA run with the same population and iterations in the experiments.

[supported] Use of a Matrix Product State (MPS) simulator is appropriate for these experiments because the generated circuits intentionally limit entanglement, enabling efficient classical simulation.

[speculative] The paper suggests that current quantum devices with ~100 qubits can begin to address utility-scale combinatorial optimization problems; this is an optimistic extrapolation from the reported experiment rather than a conclusive demonstration.
results_summary: The paper introduces EAQGA, a quantum-enhanced genetic algorithm that uses an entanglement-aware crossover to map correlated bit pairs from elite solutions into shallow quantum subcircuits, and biases unpaired qubits with single-qubit rotations. Empirical experiments on S&P 500-derived portfolio subsets (simulator: 30 and 40 assets; hardware: 100 assets on IBM ibm_quebec) show EAQGA achieves higher average fitness and lower variance than a classical GA and an adaptive quantum-inspired GA under the tested hyperparameters (20 iterations, populations 10/20). On the 100-asset hardware experiment EAQGA reported +33.6% vs GA and +37.2% vs AQGA. The authors emphasize practical NISQ suitability (limited entanglement, shallow circuits) and explicitly do not claim a formal quantum advantage.

quantum_advantage_detail: The authors explicitly state they do not claim a formal quantum advantage: EAQGA uses limited entanglement and shallow circuits which make it often classically simulable (and thus no provable asymptotic quantum speedup is claimed). Reported improvements are empirical performance gains under the tested instances and settings rather than proof of quantum computational advantage.
limitations: The authors explicitly do not claim a formal quantum advantage: the algorithm uses a limited number of entanglements and can be simulated efficiently on classical hardware.
Circuit design intentionally limits entanglement and keeps depth shallow to be NISQ-friendly, which may restrict the algorithm's ability to capture more complex multi-variable correlations.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — EAQGA reports substantial empirical improvements (≈33–37% better fitness) versus a classical GA and an adaptive quantum-inspired GA under the same population/iteration settings, including a 100-asset run on IBM's 127-qubit device.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The method is explicitly NISQ-friendly: uses shallow entanglement-aware circuits, limits chain lengths, uses an MPS simulator for low-entanglement cases, and demonstrates experiments on a real 127-qubit device (ibm_quebec).

#idea:hybrid-approach — The algorithm is hybrid: quantum circuits generate candidate bitstrings (one qubit per asset) while classical genetic operations (elitism, selection logic, fitness evaluation) and hyperparameter control steer evolution.

#limitation:noise — Hardware experiments use shots=1 per circuit and only 10 repetitions for the 100-asset hardware runs, making results susceptible to sampling noise and device errors; noise amplification risk not extensively mitigated in reported experiments.

#limitation:qubit-count — Encoding is one qubit per asset (binary inclusion), so scaling to larger asset universes requires linearly more qubits; experiments use a single 100-asset subset on a 127-qubit device, leaving broader scalability untested.
